title: Great Books · Episode 1
chapters: The dark origins of fairy tales

units.t: Great Books. Episode one.
In this episode: The great epics, The hidden shapes of stories, Shakespeare and The dark origins of fairy tales.
Part one. The great epics.
Long before novels or films, people gathered to hear poems about heroes, gods and monsters.
Some of those poems are still read, performed and argued over thousands of years later.
What makes an epic.
An epic is a long story told in verse, centred on a hero whose deeds matter to a whole community or nation.
Epics usually feature gods or supernatural forces, great journeys or wars, and big questions about fate, honour and death.
Many began as oral poetry, performed from memory by professional singers long before anyone wrote them down.
Repeated phrases, like Homer's 'rosy-fingered Dawn', helped performers keep track of thousands of lines.
Scholars distinguish these traditional epics from later 'literary' epics, written by a single known author who deliberately imitated the old style.
Gilgamesh and Homer.
The Epic of Gilgamesh comes from Mesopotamia, in modern Iraq.
Poems about Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, were written in Sumerian around 4,000 years ago.
After his friend Enkidu dies, Gilgamesh searches for eternal life and fails.
When its tablets were found at Nineveh in the 1850s, George Smith's 1872 translation of a flood story strikingly similar to Noah's caused a sensation.
The Iliad, credited to Homer, covers only a few weeks in the tenth year of the Trojan War, built around the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles.
It ends with the funeral of Hector, not the fall of Troy.
The Odyssey follows Odysseus on his ten-year journey home to Ithaca and his wife Penelope.
It gave English the word 'odyssey'.
The Aeneid.
The Roman poet Virgil wrote the Aeneid between about 29 and 19 BC, during the rule of Augustus, Rome's first emperor.

Deliberately echoing Homer, it follows Aeneas, a Trojan prince who escapes burning Troy and, after a tragic love affair with Queen Dido of Carthage, reaches Italy, where his descendants will found Rome.
The poem celebrates Rome's destiny but is haunted by the suffering that destiny demands.
Virgil died in 19 BC before finishing it and reportedly asked for the manuscript to be burned.
Augustus refused, and the Aeneid became a cornerstone of Western education for nearly 2,000 years.
Mahabharata and Beowulf.
The Mahabharata, written in Sanskrit, is often called the longest poem in the world, with around 100,000 verses in its longest versions.
Attributed to the sage Vyasa, it grew over centuries.
It tells of a bitter family conflict ending in war at Kurukshetra.
Within it sits the Bhagavad Gita, a dialogue between the warrior Arjuna and Krishna about duty and action, sacred to hundreds of millions of Hindus.
Beowulf is the most famous poem in Old English.
Though set in Scandinavia, it was written in England, with estimates of its date ranging from about AD 700 to 1000.
Beowulf kills Grendel and Grendel's mother, then dies fighting a dragon.
It survives in one manuscript, scorched in a 1731 fire in London.
Why epics endure.
Epics survive because their questions never date: how to face death, what we owe our families and communities, whether glory is worth the cost.
Their story patterns are everywhere.
Joseph Campbell argued in 1949 that many myths share a 'hero's journey', an idea that influenced Star Wars, though scholars dispute how universal it is.
R.
R. Tolkien argued that Beowulf's monsters deserved to be taken seriously, and its echoes run through The Hobbit.
Oral storytelling is also a living tradition in Australia, where Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have passed stories down over many generations.
To try an epic, start with a modern translation, such as Emily Wilson's 2017 Odyssey, or an audiobook.
These poems were made to be heard.
The key idea: An epic is a long verse story about a hero whose deeds matter to a whole community, and many began as oral poetry.
Part two. The hidden shapes of stories.
Is there really only a handful of plots in the world?
Writers and scientists have long tried to map the hidden structures beneath the stories we love.
Early maps of plot.
Think of almost any film you have enjoyed.
Someone wants something, obstacles appear, things get worse, then there is a turning point and a resolution.
It feels natural, but people have tried to describe the pattern for over two thousand years.
In his Poetics, in the 4th century BCE, Aristotle observed that a good tragedy has a beginning, a middle and an end, and its events follow from one another by necessity or probability.
A plot is a chain of causes, not a list of events.
In 1863 the German critic Gustav Freytag drew drama as a five-part pyramid: introduction, rising action, climax, falling action and catastrophe or resolution.
It fits tragedies like Hamlet well, but suits many modern stories less well.
The hero's journey.
In 1949 the American scholar Joseph Campbell published The Hero with a Thousand Faces.
Drawing on myths from many cultures, he argued that hero stories often follow a similar path, which he called the monomyth.
A hero leaves the ordinary world after a call to adventure, often helped by a mentor.
The hero crosses into an unfamiliar world, faces trials and a great ordeal, gains a reward or insight, and returns home transformed.
Campbell became enormously influential in Hollywood.
George Lucas has said his work shaped Star Wars, and screenwriters later popularised the pattern as a practical template.
Critics argue Campbell picked examples that fit and ignored many that do not, but the idea remains widely used.
Counting the plots.

In 2004 the British journalist Christopher Booker published The Seven Basic Plots, arguing that stories fall into types such as overcoming the monster, rags to riches, the quest, comedy, tragedy and rebirth.
Others propose anywhere from three to over thirty.
Jaws and David and Goliath really are both about overcoming a monster.
But critics say the categories are so broad that almost anything fits.
Kurt Vonnegut drew stories as lines on a graph, with good fortune up and bad fortune down.
In 2016 US researchers analysed the emotional words in over 1,000 works of fiction and reported six basic emotional arcs.
Like all such studies, it is open to debate.
Other storytelling traditions.
Most of these models come from European and American traditions and assume stories are driven by conflict between a hero and an obstacle.
Other traditions work differently.

A classical structure from Chinese poetry, later used in Japanese and Korean storytelling and often called kishotenketsu in Japanese, has four parts: introduction, development, a twist and a conclusion that brings the parts together.
The twist need not be a conflict, just a surprising new angle.
Aboriginal storytelling traditions are often closely tied to land and place, and many stories connect to particular sites and to responsibilities for Country, rather than following one hero's arc.
These differences remind us that the Western plot is one model among many.
Why structure matters.
Knowing these patterns does not mean every story must follow them.
Many great books play with structure: they start at the end, tell events out of order, or refuse a tidy resolution.
But understanding the common shapes is useful.
As a reader, it helps you notice why a story feels satisfying or why it drags.
As a writer, it gives you questions to ask: what does the main character want, what stands in the way, and what changes by the end?
Psychologists have also found that people tend to remember information better when it is told as a story with causes and consequences.
That may be why the same shapes keep appearing, from campfire tales to streaming series.
We seem to think in stories.
The key idea: Thinkers from Aristotle to Freytag described plot as a chain of causes that rises and falls.
Part three. Shakespeare.
A glove-maker's son from a small market town wrote plays that are still performed around the world, and he put words in your mouth you didn't know were his.
A Stratford boy.
William Shakespeare was baptised in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564.
His father John was a glove-maker who became a local official.
At 18 William married Anne Hathaway, who was 26.
They had three children: Susanna, then twins Hamnet and Judith.
Hamnet died in 1596, aged 11.
Surprisingly little is known about his personal life, and the records have a gap from about 1585 to 1592 that scholars call 'the lost years'.
By 1592 he was working in London, where rival Robert Greene mocked him as an 'upstart crow'.
Unusually, he was actor, writer and part-owner of his company, which made him fairly wealthy.
The Globe and the Folio.
He became a leading member of the Lord Chamberlain's Men, which became the King's Men after James I took the throne in 1603.
In 1599 the company built the Globe Theatre on the south bank of the Thames.
It burned down in 1613 when a cannon fired during a performance set the thatched roof alight.
A reconstruction opened near the site in 1997.
Shakespeare is credited with about 37 plays and 154 sonnets.
Many plays were never printed in his lifetime.
In 1623 two fellow actors, John Heminges and Henry Condell, published 36 of them in the First Folio.
About 18, including Macbeth and The Tempest, had never been printed and might otherwise have vanished.
About 235 copies survive, including one in Sydney's State Library of NSW.
Tragedy, comedy and history.
His tragedies follow powerful people destroyed by their own choices, flaws or circumstances.
Hamlet agonises over revenge.
Macbeth, spurred by a prophecy and his wife's ambition, spirals into tyranny.
Othello is manipulated by Iago into jealousy and murder.
King Lear divides his kingdom and is betrayed.
Characters think aloud in soliloquies, letting us overhear their minds.
The comedies, such as A Midsummer Night's Dream and Twelfth Night, feature mistaken identities, disguises and happy endings, usually weddings.
Because women could not act on the English stage, boys played female roles.
The histories, including Richard III and Henry V, shaped popular ideas of English kings far more than historians would like.
Late plays like The Tempest are often called romances: stories of loss, magic and forgiveness.
Words and verse.
The Oxford English Dictionary lists Shakespeare as the earliest known source for many words, such as 'eyeball', 'bedroom' and 'swagger', though some were probably already in speech.
Phrases first found in his plays include 'wild-goose chase', Romeo and Juliet, 'green-eyed monster' and 'a foregone conclusion', both Othello.
Much of his writing is blank verse: unrhymed lines of iambic pentameter.
That is ten syllables with an unstressed-stressed beat, da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM, close to natural speech.
Kings and lovers tend to speak in verse, servants and comic characters in prose.
A rhyming couplet often closes a scene, like a musical full stop.
Reading aloud makes the lines easier to follow.
Why he lasts.
Shakespeare's plays survive because they deal with things that never go away: ambition, jealousy, love, grief, power and family conflict.
They are also endlessly adaptable.
West Side Story reworks Romeo and Juliet, 10 Things I Hate About You updates The Taming of the Shrew, and The Lion King borrows from Hamlet.
Australian director Baz Luhrmann's Romeo + Juliet, 1996, kept the original language in a modern setting.
Bell Shakespeare, founded by John Bell in 1990, tours his plays around Australia.
The best way in is to watch a performance first.
These were scripts for actors, not texts for exams.
The key idea: Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564, became a London actor, writer and shareholder, and little is known of his private life.
Part four. The dark origins of fairy tales.
Before Disney, Cinderella's stepsisters cut off parts of their feet to fit the slipper.
Fairy tales have a long, strange and sometimes gruesome history.
Older than writing.
Long before anyone wrote them down, fairy tales were told aloud, by grandparents at the fire, by workers passing the time and by nurses to children.
They were not just for kids.
Adults told tales of clever peasants, cruel stepmothers and magical helpers to entertain each other and pass on lessons.
Because the tales lived in memory, they changed with each teller and crossed borders.
Folklorists catalogue thousands of tale types in the Aarne-Thompson-Uther index.
Cinderella is a good example.
The Greek writer Strabo recorded the story of Rhodopis, whose sandal an eagle dropped in an Egyptian king's lap.
A 9th-century Chinese tale tells of Ye Xian, helped by a fish's bones, who loses a golden shoe.
Perrault and Basile.
In 1697, Charles Perrault, a member of the French Academy, published a small book of tales that included 'Cinderella', 'Sleeping Beauty', 'Little Red Riding Hood' and 'Puss in Boots'.
He polished folk tales for fashionable readers at the court of Louis XIV, adding wit and ending each tale with a little moral in verse.
Perrault gave us the pumpkin coach and the glass slipper.
His Red Riding Hood ends badly: the wolf eats her, and no woodcutter arrives.
The moral warns young women about smooth-talking men.
Earlier, in the 1630s, the Italian writer Giambattista Basile had published his own collection, including early versions of Cinderella and Sleeping Beauty.
The Brothers Grimm.
In 1812, the German scholars Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm published the first volume of their Children's and Household Tales.
They were language experts who wanted to preserve what they saw as the authentic voice of the German people, at a time when Germany was divided and occupied by Napoleon's France.
Their image of peasants telling ancient tales is a little misleading.
Many storytellers were educated, middle-class young women, some of French Huguenot descent, who already knew Perrault's tales.
One prized source, Dorothea Viehmann, was a tailor's widow with a vast memory for stories.
The brothers revised the collection repeatedly, and the final edition of 1857 held around 200 tales.
Softer, but bloodier.
The first Grimm edition was not a children's book, and parents complained.
So Wilhelm in particular reworked the tales for family reading.
Sexual hints went.
In the first 'Rapunzel', the witch discovers the prince's visits when Rapunzel innocently remarks that her clothes are getting tight around her waist.
Later editions changed this to a harmless slip of the tongue.
Evil mothers were often turned into stepmothers, to protect the ideal of motherhood.
Violence mostly stayed, because it punished wickedness.
In the Grimms' Cinderella, the stepsisters cut off a toe and a heel to fit the slipper, and at the wedding, birds peck out their eyes.
Andersen and endurance.
Hans Christian Andersen mostly invented new tales, starting in 1835: 'The Little Mermaid', 'The Ugly Duckling', 'The Emperor's New Clothes' and 'The Snow Queen'.
In his original 'Little Mermaid', the prince marries someone else.
She refuses to kill him to save herself and dissolves into foam, becoming a spirit of the air.
Many readers see Andersen's own loneliness in his stories.
Fairy tales keep returning because they deal with growing up, injustice, luck and courage.
In 1976 Bruno Bettelheim argued that their frightening parts help children face fears safely, though his ideas are debated.
A 2016 study suggested some tales may be thousands of years old, though such estimates are uncertain.
The key idea: Fairy tales began as spoken folk tales, and Cinderella-type stories have been told around the world for well over a thousand years.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did oral epics use repeated phrases like 'rosy-fingered Dawn'?
Answer. They helped singers remember the lines.
Question two. What was Aristotle's key point about plot?
Answer. Events should follow from one another as a chain of causes.
Question three. What made Shakespeare unusual among playwrights of his day?
Answer. He acted, wrote and part-owned a company.
Question four. Why do very similar fairy tales appear in many different countries?
Answer. Spoken tales changed with each teller and crossed borders.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
